description: How full your nodes are by what pods ask for: each node's allocatable CPU and memory (/api/v1/nodes) against the summed requests of the pods placed on it (/api/v1/pods, not finished ones). The scheduler packs by requests, not by usage, so this is the room that is left for new pods. Statistics: utilisation is a distribution over nodes, and free capacity only counts where it fits. A node full on CPU but half empty on memory strands that memory (the scatter, off its diagonal); total free CPU is spread over nodes, and a pod larger than the biggest single gap stays Pending though the cluster as a whole has room. The last graph counts how many more "typical" pods (the median request) fit on each node and which resource stops it. Hover a node for its requests, pods and kubelet version. Caveats: init containers, pod overhead and DaemonSets yet to start are not counted; containers without a request count as 0, and limits are not shown; up to 500 pods (limit=500). Needs signing in and a connected cluster: the datasource is https://kubernetes.default.svc, the in-cluster address of the Kubernetes API, reached through your organization's own Seebra gateway running in that cluster (Settings → Organization), with a read-only service-account token kept in the gateway's Secret under the name k8s-token (sent as a bearer token). Signed out, or through Seebra's hosted gateway, no cluster can be reached, so this example shows errors there. The datasource shows "key ?" because the token lives on the gateway, not among your Seebra secrets. Setup, RBAC and the kubectl proxy route: docs, Use cases → Kubernetes.
name: Kubernetes capacity and bin-packing
